result:
There is a quiet miracle in how human beings store time. Not in clocks or calendars, but in objects. A chipped mug that reminds you of a winter kitchen. A song that instantly rebuilds a summer you had forgotten. A book with a cracked spine that still smells like the year you first read it. We are not good at holding time inside ourselves — it slips, it blurs — so we outsource it to the world around us.

I think this is why we love libraries and museums and old photographs. They are not about the past. They are about proof. Proof that we were here, that we felt things, that moments mattered enough to be saved. Every shelf is an argument against forgetting.

And yet, the most precious storage is other people. The way your old friend remembers the exact joke you told ten years ago. The way a mother remembers how her child liked his sandwiches cut. The way strangers on a train briefly share a laugh and carry it with them for the rest of the day without ever knowing each other's names.

We are, all of us, walking archives. Fragile, imperfect, beautifully annotated. We leak and fade and misremember, but we keep trying to preserve what loves us. Maybe that is the whole task of a life: to decide what is worth carrying forward, and to carry it gently. Not perfectly, not forever, but with enough care that someone else might carry it onward too.
